about: Public Sector Economics (POLS0081) is a 15-credit Term 2 module in UCL's Department of Political Science, open only to first-year BSc Politics and International Relations students. Per the 2026/27 catalogue it introduces economic principles for studying politics and public policy to students with little or no economics background, asks how policymakers can use economic insights, and encourages critical scrutiny of the assumptions behind economics, and of the links between politics and economics. The catalogue lists the topics as markets and market failures, efficiency and equity, policy evaluation, trade, and recent developments in public economics; this pack follows that order, splitting the first topic into two notes. Teaching is by lectures and seminars, and assessment is 100% exam (2026/27); no week-by-week reading list is published in the catalogue, so the examples here are standard ones chosen to fit each topic.
topics: Markets and market failures: how markets work
Markets and market failures: why markets fail

notes.h: How markets work: demand, supply and surplus
notes.body:
Economics gives political scientists a toolkit for asking what a policy will do, who gains and who loses. The starting point is the competitive market.

Thinking like an economist
- People respond to incentives: if something becomes more costly, they tend to do less of it.
- Every choice has an opportunity cost, the value of the best alternative given up. A council that spends £1m on a new library cannot spend it on road repairs.
- Decisions are made at the margin: compare the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost.
- Models simplify on purpose. A good critic asks which assumptions matter for the conclusion, not whether the model is literally true.

Demand and supply
- The demand curve shows how much buyers want at each price. It slopes downward because, as price rises, people switch to substitutes and can afford less.
- The supply curve shows how much sellers will offer at each price. It slopes upward because producing more usually raises marginal cost.
- Equilibrium is where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. If the price is above it there is a surplus and sellers cut prices; below it there is a shortage and prices are bid up.
- Movements along a curve come from a change in the good's own price. Shifts come from other factors: income, tastes or the price of related goods (demand); input costs or technology (supply).

Elasticity
- Price elasticity of demand = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.
- Demand is inelastic (|elasticity| < 1) for goods with few substitutes, such as fuel or cigarettes in the short run, and elastic for goods with close substitutes.
- Elasticity matters for policy: taxing an inelastic good raises a lot of revenue but changes behaviour little; taxing an elastic good changes behaviour more.

Surplus and efficiency
- Consumer surplus is the difference between what buyers would be willing to pay and what they actually pay, summed over all units: the area under the demand curve and above the price.
- Producer surplus is the difference between the price and the sellers' marginal cost: the area above the supply curve and below the price.
- In a competitive market without failures, equilibrium maximises total surplus. Every unit worth more to a buyer than it costs to make is traded, and none that is worth less.

Interfering with prices
- A binding price ceiling (such as rent control set below the market rent) creates a shortage: quantity supplied falls, and the good must be rationed by queues, connections or quality.
- A binding price floor (such as a minimum wage above the market wage in a competitive labour market) creates excess supply. In labour markets where employers have wage-setting power (monopsony), a moderate minimum wage can raise both pay and employment, which is one reason the evidence on minimum wages is debated.
- At the time of writing (October 2026), the UK National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over is £12.71 an hour, in force since 1 April 2026; check GOV.UK for later rates.

Taxes and deadweight loss
- Example: demand P = 50 − Q and supply P = 10 + Q give Q = 20 and P = 30.
- An £8 tax per unit on sellers gives 50 − Q = 18 + Q, so Q = 16. Buyers pay £34, sellers keep £26 and revenue is 8 × 16 = £128.
- The deadweight loss is ½ × 8 × (20 − 16) = £16: the surplus lost on trades that no longer happen.
- Who bears a tax depends on elasticities, not on who legally pays it. Here the burden is split equally because the curves have equal slopes.

Exam tips: draw and label a diagram for every market question, state which curve shifts and why, and use surplus areas to judge efficiency.

notes.h: Why markets fail and what governments can do
notes.body:
The case for government intervention in public economics usually starts from a market failure: a situation in which the market outcome is inefficient, so that some change could make someone better off without making anyone worse off.

1. Externalities
- An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside a transaction.
- Negative externalities (pollution, congestion, second-hand smoke) are overproduced, because the producer or consumer ignores the cost to others: marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost.
- Positive externalities (vaccination, education, research) are underproduced.
- Remedies:
  - A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external damage, named after Arthur Pigou (The Economics of Welfare, 1920). UK policies that use this logic include fuel duty (partly) and the single-use carrier bag charge in England (5p from October 2015, 10p from May 2021), although the bag charge is kept by retailers rather than paid to government as a tax.
  - Subsidies for positive externalities.
  - Regulation and standards, such as emission limits.
  - Tradable permits, as in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (from 2021).
  - Private bargaining: Ronald Coase (1960) argued that with clear property rights and low bargaining costs, the parties can reach an efficient outcome themselves. This rarely works when many people are affected.

2. Public goods
- A pure public good is non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people cannot be stopped from using it): national defence, flood defences, street lighting.
- Markets under-supply public goods because people can free ride on others' payments, which is why they are usually financed by taxation.
- Common-pool resources (fish stocks, groundwater) are rival but non-excludable and tend to be overused. Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can sometimes manage them with their own rules.

3. Imperfect and asymmetric information
- Adverse selection (hidden characteristics): in George Akerlof's market for lemons (1970), buyers cannot tell good used cars from bad, so they will pay only an average price, good cars are withdrawn, and the market can unravel. In insurance, if only high-risk people buy cover, premiums rise and low-risk people drop out. Compulsory insurance (for example motor insurance) or public provision can help.
- Moral hazard (hidden actions): insured people may take less care, and banks that expect to be rescued may take more risk.

4. Market power
- Monopolies and cartels raise prices above marginal cost and restrict output, creating a deadweight loss. Competition law (enforced in the UK by the Competition and Markets Authority) and the regulation of natural monopolies such as water are the responses.

5. Incomplete markets and macroeconomic instability
- Some markets do not exist or work badly (long-term care insurance, lending to people without collateral). Recessions leave resources idle, which supports stabilisation policy.

Government failure
Market failure is necessary but not sufficient for intervention. Governments may also fail: they lack information, respond to lobbying (regulatory capture), are short-termist around elections, or create unintended incentives. Public choice theory applies economic reasoning to politicians and bureaucrats, assuming they too pursue their own interests. The right comparison is between an imperfect market and an imperfect government.

Exam tips: identify the specific failure, explain the mechanism (whose cost or benefit is ignored, and why), and weigh at least two policy responses including the risk of government failure.

Public economics constantly weighs two goals: making the economy as productive as possible (efficiency) and distributing its fruits fairly (equity). Economics can clarify the trade-offs; it cannot by itself decide how much weight to put on each.

Efficiency
- An allocation is Pareto efficient if no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
- Under ideal conditions a competitive market equilibrium is Pareto efficient (the first fundamental theorem of welfare economics).
- The second welfare theorem says that, under the same ideal conditions, any Pareto-efficient allocation can be reached by a competitive market after suitable lump-sum redistribution. In practice lump-sum transfers based on ability are impossible, so redistribution uses taxes on income or spending that change behaviour.
- Pareto efficiency says nothing about fairness: an allocation in which one person owns everything can be efficient.

Equity
- Horizontal equity: people in similar circumstances should be treated similarly.
- Vertical equity: people with greater ability to pay should pay more.
- Measures of inequality include the Gini coefficient (0 = complete equality, 1 = one person has everything) and ratios such as the income share of the top 1%.

Social welfare functions
- A utilitarian social welfare function adds up individuals' utilities. With diminishing marginal utility, £1,000 moved from a richer to a poorer person raises total welfare: with logarithmic utility, it is worth about 0.11 to someone on £9,000 but only about 0.05 to someone on £20,000.
- A Rawlsian (maximin) function, from John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971), judges society by the welfare of its worst-off member.
- Other views stress rights, procedures or equality of opportunity rather than outcomes.

The equity–efficiency trade-off
- Redistribution usually requires taxes and means-tested benefits, which change incentives to work, save and invest. Arthur Okun (Equality and Efficiency: The Big Tradeoff, 1975) likened this to carrying money in a "leaky bucket": some is lost on the way.
- How much leaks depends on how responsive people are to taxes (elasticities), on how taxes are designed and on what the revenue funds. Spending on education or health can increase future productivity, so not every redistribution reduces efficiency.

Marginal and average tax rates (England, Wales and Northern Ireland, 2026/27 rates at the time of writing, October 2026)
- Personal Allowance £12,570; basic rate 20% up to £50,270; higher rate 40% up to £125,140; additional rate 45% above. Scotland sets its own bands.
- Someone earning £60,000 pays 20% × £37,700 + 40% × £9,730 = £11,432: an average rate of 19.05% but a marginal rate of 40%.
- The Personal Allowance is withdrawn at £1 for every £2 of income above £100,000, so between £100,000 and £125,140 each extra pound faces an effective marginal rate of 60% (40% plus 40% of the 50p of allowance lost).
- Universal Credit is withdrawn at 55p for every £1 earned above any work allowance (the taper at the time of writing, October 2026); combined with income tax and National Insurance, this gives low earners high effective marginal rates.
- Incentives depend on the marginal rate; the distributional burden is better shown by the average rate.

Excess burden
- A tax costs society more than the revenue it raises because it distorts choices. This excess burden (deadweight loss) rises with the square of the tax rate in simple models, so a few high rates are more costly than many low ones.
- Taxes on inelastic bases (such as land) create small deadweight losses.

Exam tips: separate positive claims (what a tax does) from normative ones (whether it is fair), and use average and marginal rates correctly when discussing incentives and fairness.

Governments need to know whether a policy is worth doing before it starts (appraisal) and whether it worked afterwards (evaluation). Economics supplies two main tools: cost–benefit analysis and causal impact evaluation.

Cost–benefit analysis (CBA)
- List everyone affected and value the costs and benefits in money, including effects that are not traded in markets (time saved, lives saved, environmental damage).
- Non-market values are estimated from behaviour (revealed preference, for example how house prices vary with noise) or surveys (stated preference, willingness to pay).
- In the UK, HM Treasury's Green Book sets the rules for appraising public spending.

Discounting
- Benefits that arrive later are worth less today. Present value PV = amount ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate and t the number of years.
- Net present value (NPV) = PV of benefits − PV of costs. A positive NPV means the project passes the test.
- The Green Book's standard real discount rate has been 3.5% a year since 2003, falling for very long-term effects, with a lower rate for health effects. An independent review commissioned by HM Treasury, published on 30 June 2026, recommended cutting the standard rate to 3%. At the time of writing (October 2026) the Treasury had not announced whether it will adopt this, so check the current Green Book.
- The rate matters a great deal: £1m received in 50 years is worth about £179,000 today at 3.5% and £228,000 at 3%.
- Worked example: a project costs £100m now and yields £12m a year for 10 years. At 3.5% the benefits are worth £99.8m, so NPV ≈ −£0.2m and the project just fails; at 3% they are worth £102.4m, so NPV ≈ +£2.4m and it passes.
- Choosing the discount rate is partly an ethical question about how to weigh future generations, which is central to climate policy.

Distribution in CBA
- Standard CBA adds up money values regardless of who receives them. Distributional weights can give more weight to gains for poorer people, reflecting diminishing marginal utility of income.

Impact evaluation: did it work?
The fundamental problem is the counterfactual: we cannot observe what would have happened to the same people without the policy.
- Before-and-after comparisons confuse the policy with everything else that changed at the same time.
- Comparing participants with non-participants suffers from selection bias, because people who choose to take part differ.

Methods that tackle this:
- Randomised controlled trials (RCTs): randomly assign who gets the policy, so the groups are alike on average. The UK's Behavioural Insights Team, set up in the Cabinet Office in 2010, has used trials to test letters encouraging people to pay tax on time.
- Difference-in-differences: compare the change over time in a treated group with the change in an untreated group; assumes they would otherwise have followed parallel trends. Card and Krueger (1994) used this to compare fast-food employment in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage, with neighbouring Pennsylvania, and found no fall in employment.
- Regression discontinuity: compare people just above and just below an eligibility cut-off.
- Natural experiments: exploit events that change exposure to a policy for reasons unrelated to outcomes.

Judging the evidence
- Internal validity: is the effect correctly estimated for the people studied?
- External validity: would it work elsewhere, at scale or for different groups?
- Politics matters: evidence competes with values, interests and timing, and pilots may be judged on political rather than evidential grounds.

Exam tips: in any evaluation question, say what the counterfactual is, explain how the method constructs it and name the key assumption; in CBA questions, show the discounting and test how sensitive the answer is to the discount rate.

notes.h: The economics and politics of trade
notes.body:
International trade is a classic case where economic analysis shows aggregate gains while political analysis explains why trade is contested.

Comparative advantage
- David Ricardo (On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, 1817) showed that countries gain from specialising in goods for which they have the lower opportunity cost, even if one country is better at producing everything (absolute advantage).
- Example: the UK needs 2 hours to make a unit of cloth and 6 hours for a unit of wine; France needs 4 and 8. The UK is better at both, but a unit of wine costs it 3 units of cloth, while in France it costs only 2. France has a comparative advantage in wine and the UK in cloth.
- If they trade at any price between 2 and 3 units of cloth per unit of wine, both can consume more than they could alone.

Other reasons for trade
- Economies of scale and product variety explain why similar countries trade similar goods (cars for cars).
- Competition from imports lowers prices and pressures firms to become more efficient.

Who gains and who loses
- Gains from trade are aggregate: consumers and exporting industries gain, while workers and firms in import-competing industries can lose.
- The Stolper–Samuelson theorem predicts that trade raises the real return to a country's abundant factor and lowers the return to its scarce factor. In rich countries with relatively little low-skilled labour, that means pressure on low-skilled wages.
- Losses are concentrated geographically. Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2013) found that US local labour markets more exposed to rising Chinese imports suffered larger falls in manufacturing employment, higher unemployment, lower wages and higher take-up of benefits; later work by the same authors found these effects persisted for years.
- In principle the winners could compensate the losers, but in practice compensation is often limited.

Trade policy tools
- A tariff is a tax on imports. For a small country that cannot affect world prices, a tariff raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, reduces consumption and imports, and raises revenue.
- Worked example: domestic demand Qd = 120 − P, domestic supply Qs = P, world price £20. With free trade the country consumes 100, produces 20 and imports 80. A £10 tariff raises the price to £30: consumption 90, production 30, imports 60.
  - Consumer surplus falls by 10 × (100 + 90)/2 = £950.
  - Producer surplus rises by 10 × (20 + 30)/2 = £250.
  - Tariff revenue is 10 × 60 = £600.
  - Net loss = 950 − 250 − 600 = £100, made up of a production distortion (½ × 10 × 10 = 50) and a consumption distortion (50).
- Quotas have similar effects but the revenue goes to whoever holds the import licences. Non-tariff barriers such as differing regulations, customs checks and rules of origin can also raise costs.

The political economy of protection
- The benefits of protection are concentrated on a few organised producers, while the costs are spread thinly over many consumers. Mancur Olson's logic of collective action (1965) predicts that concentrated interests lobby more effectively, so protection is more common than the efficiency analysis would suggest.
- Arguments for protection include infant industries, national security, retaliation and strategic trade policy, but each carries a risk of capture by special interests.
- Trade agreements commit governments to lower barriers, helping them resist lobbying.

UK context
The UK left the EU's single market and customs union at the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020. The UK–EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement keeps tariff-free, quota-free trade in goods that meet its rules of origin, but customs and regulatory checks raised trade costs, especially for small firms.

Exam tips: compute opportunity costs carefully to identify comparative advantage, draw the tariff diagram with all four areas, and connect who gains and loses to the politics of trade policy.

Public economics has changed in recent decades through behavioural economics, new data and better evidence about taxes and transfers. These developments question some textbook assumptions, which the module encourages students to do.

Behavioural public economics
- Standard models assume people are fully rational, with stable preferences and unlimited attention. Evidence from psychology and experiments shows systematic departures: present bias (overweighting today against the future), loss aversion, inertia, limited attention and social influences.
- Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein (Nudge, 2008) argued that the way choices are presented, the "choice architecture", can steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice.
- Defaults are powerful: Madrian and Shea (2001) showed that automatically enrolling US employees in a workplace pension plan sharply increased participation.
- In the UK, automatic enrolment into workplace pensions was introduced under the Pensions Act 2008 and rolled out from October 2012, starting with the largest employers. Eligible employees are enrolled unless they opt out, and minimum total contributions have been 8% of qualifying earnings, at least 3% from the employer, since April 2019. Participation rose sharply.
- The Behavioural Insights Team, set up in the Cabinet Office in 2010, tested messages such as telling late taxpayers that most people in their area pay on time, which increased payment rates in trials.
- Behavioural ideas also matter for taxes: people respond more to taxes that are visible or salient.

Critiques of nudging
- Nudges are cheap but often have modest effects, and some have not replicated at scale.
- Who decides what counts as a good choice? Critics see paternalism and possible manipulation.
- Nudges may distract from structural policies such as taxes, regulation or public provision.

New data and inequality
- Administrative tax records have transformed the measurement of top incomes. Piketty and Saez (2003) used US tax data to show that the top income share fell in the mid twentieth century and rose sharply from the 1980s; similar series exist for the UK.
- Large linked data sets let researchers study social mobility by place. Chetty and co-authors (2014) found large differences in upward mobility between US areas.

Optimal taxation of top incomes
- The optimal top tax rate depends on how strongly taxable income responds to the tax rate (the elasticity of taxable income) and on how thick the top tail of the income distribution is.
- Diamond and Saez (2011) suggested a revenue-maximising top rate of about 73% under their central assumptions. Critics point out that the elasticity is higher when people can move income between tax years, between types of income or abroad, so design (closing avoidance routes) matters as much as the rate.
- UK evidence that taxpayers moved income into or out of particular tax years when the 50% additional rate was introduced (2010) and cut to 45% (2013) illustrates these timing responses.

Other active debates
- The design of means-tested benefits, such as the Universal Credit taper of 55p per £1 earned, and its effects on work incentives.
- Wealth and property taxation, including council tax bands that in England still rest on 1991 valuations.
- Carbon pricing and how to make it fair to low-income households.
- Using RCTs and natural experiments ("what works") to evaluate policy.

Thinking critically
Economic reasoning is a way of asking questions: what are the incentives, who gains and loses, and what is the evidence? But its assumptions, especially about rationality, measurement and value judgements, should be scrutinised rather than accepted.

Exam tips: present each new idea with its evidence and a critique, and connect it back to the efficiency and equity framework.

questions.q: Demand is P = 50 − Q and supply is P = 10 + Q. A tax of £8 per unit is imposed on sellers. What are the tax revenue and the deadweight loss?
questions.why: With the tax, 50 − Q = 18 + Q gives Q = 16, so revenue is 8 × 16 = £128 and the deadweight loss is ½ × 8 × (20 − 16) = £16. £160 multiplies the tax by the original quantity of 20, forgetting that the tax reduces sales. £32 forgets the ½ in the area of the triangle. A zero deadweight loss would require quantity not to fall, which happens only if demand or supply is perfectly inelastic.

questions.q: A city sets maximum rents well below the market rent. What does the basic supply and demand model predict?
options: Higher rents in the controlled sector
A shortage of rental housing, with fewer flats supplied than tenants want
A surplus of empty rental flats
No change in quantity, because housing supply is fixed
questions.why: A ceiling below equilibrium increases quantity demanded and reduces quantity supplied, so a shortage results. A surplus is what a price floor above equilibrium creates, not a ceiling. Fixed supply is true only in the very short run; over time landlords convert or sell properties, so the quantity supplied falls. Rents cannot rise in the controlled sector because the ceiling is binding.

questions.q: Explain, using a supply and demand diagram, how a per-unit tax on a good affects the price paid by buyers, the price received by sellers, the quantity traded and economic efficiency.
markScheme: Tax shifts supply up by the amount of the tax (or creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices)
Buyers pay more and sellers receive less than before; quantity falls
Incidence depends on relative elasticities, not on who legally pays
Revenue = tax × new quantity (rectangle)
Deadweight loss triangle from trades no longer made; larger when demand/supply are more elastic
questions.modelAnswer: A tax of t per unit drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive: the supply curve shifts up by t. The new equilibrium has a higher buyer price, a lower seller price and a smaller quantity. The split of the tax depends on elasticities: if demand is less elastic than supply, buyers bear most of it. Revenue is the rectangle t × new quantity. The units no longer traded were worth more to buyers than they cost to produce, so their lost surplus is a deadweight loss triangle. The more elastic demand or supply is, the more the quantity falls and the larger the deadweight loss.

questions.q: Why does a private insurance market for a risk where customers know their own risk better than insurers tend to work badly?
options: A negative externality: one person's insurance raises others' premiums automatically
Adverse selection: high-risk people are keener to buy, so premiums rise and low-risk people leave
Moral hazard: buyers choose risky behaviour before they know whether they are insured
It is a public good, so nobody can be excluded from cover
questions.why: When insurers cannot tell high-risk from low-risk customers, they price for the average; low-risk people find this poor value and leave, pushing premiums up further. That is adverse selection, a problem of hidden characteristics. Moral hazard concerns hidden actions taken after cover is bought, not who chooses to buy. Insurance is excludable, since people without a policy are not paid out, so it is not a public good. The rise in premiums comes from the pool's composition, not from an externality one buyer imposes on another.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of a pure public good?
options: A subsidised university place
A council swimming pool that charges entry
A flood defence protecting a whole town
A fish stock in open international waters
questions.why: Flood defences protect everyone in the area, and protecting one household does not reduce the protection of others: non-rival and non-excludable. A swimming pool that charges entry is excludable, and it becomes rival when crowded. An open-sea fish stock is non-excludable but rival, which makes it a common-pool resource. A university place is both rival and excludable; it may be publicly funded, but public funding does not make something a public good.

questions.q: Using one example, explain why markets under-provide public goods, and explain why the existence of a market failure does not by itself justify government intervention.
markScheme: Defines public good: non-rival and non-excludable, with a valid example
Free riding: people can benefit without paying, so private provision or voluntary contributions are too low
Hence tax-financed public provision (or compulsory funding)
Government failure: limited information, lobbying/capture, electoral incentives, cost of intervention
Need to compare the imperfect market with an imperfect government; intervention justified only if it improves on the market
questions.modelAnswer: Street lighting is non-rival, because one person's use does not reduce anyone else's, and non-excludable, because it is impractical to stop passers-by benefiting. A private firm could not charge for it, and if residents were asked to contribute voluntarily, each would hope others paid, so contributions would fall short of the value to everyone. This free-rider problem is why such goods are usually financed by taxation. But market failure alone does not justify intervention: governments may not know how much people value the good, may be influenced by lobby groups or electoral timing, and raise their funds through distorting taxes. Intervention is justified only if, after these costs, it is expected to do better than the imperfect market.

questions.q: In 2026/27 someone in England earns £60,000 from employment. What are their income tax bill and marginal income tax rate?
questions.why: Tax is 20% of the £37,700 basic-rate band (£7,540) plus 40% of £9,730 (£3,892), totalling £11,432, and the next pound is taxed at 40%. £24,000 applies 40% to the whole income, ignoring the allowance and the basic-rate band. 19% is the average rate (11,432 ÷ 60,000), not the marginal rate. £9,486 taxes all income above the Personal Allowance at the basic rate of 20%, ignoring the 40% rate on income above £50,270.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects a Rawlsian approach to judging a policy?
options: Prefer any policy that is a Pareto improvement, and treat all others as equally good
Prefer the policy that maximises GDP
Prefer the policy that most improves the position of the worst-off person
Prefer the policy that maximises the sum of everyone's utility
questions.why: Rawls's maximin principle ranks outcomes by the welfare of the worst-off member of society. Maximising the sum of utilities is utilitarianism, which can accept losses for the poorest if gains elsewhere are larger. The Pareto criterion cannot rank most real policies, which have losers, and it says nothing about distribution. Maximising GDP ignores distribution altogether and is not a Rawlsian criterion.

questions.q: Explain the equity–efficiency trade-off in redistribution, and illustrate it using the withdrawal of the Personal Allowance above £100,000 or the Universal Credit taper.
markScheme: Redistribution uses distortionary taxes/means-tested benefits; lump-sum transfers not feasible
Incentive effects reduce work/earnings, so total surplus falls (Okun's leaky bucket); size depends on elasticities
Example: allowance taper gives 60% effective marginal rate between £100,000 and £125,140 (40% + half of allowance taxed at 40%)
Or: UC taper of 55p per £1 earned plus tax and NI means low earners keep a small share of extra earnings
Recognises the trade-off is a matter of degree and design, and that normative judgements decide the balance
questions.modelAnswer: Redistribution has to be financed by taxes and delivered through means-tested benefits, because lump-sum transfers based on ability are not feasible. Both change incentives: higher marginal tax rates and benefit withdrawal reduce the gain from working or earning more, so some of the money transferred is lost through lower activity, Okun's leaky bucket. How large the leak is depends on how responsive people are. The withdrawal of the Personal Allowance at £1 for every £2 above £100,000 means that each extra pound in that range is taxed at 40% and also removes 50p of allowance, which is then taxed at 40%, an effective 60% marginal rate. Similarly, Universal Credit is withdrawn at 55p per £1 earned, so after income tax and National Insurance a low earner keeps only a small share of extra pay. Design choices such as the taper rate set the balance between targeting help and preserving incentives; how much efficiency to trade for equity is a normative choice.

questions.q: A project costs £100m today and yields £12m a year for 10 years, starting next year. Using a 3.5% discount rate, the NPV is about −£0.2m; at 3% it is about +£2.4m. What is the best conclusion?
options: The project should go ahead because its undiscounted benefits (£120m) exceed its cost
The project fails at any discount rate because its NPV at 3.5% is negative
Discounting does not matter because the project lasts only 10 years
The decision is sensitive to the discount rate, so the choice of rate needs justifying
questions.why: The NPV changes sign between 3.5% and 3%, so the result depends on the discount rate and should be tested for sensitivity. Comparing £120m with £100m ignores discounting altogether, treating future money as worth the same as money today. Failing at 3.5% does not mean failing at every rate: the NPV at 3% is positive. Ten years is long enough for discounting to turn £120m into roughly £100m in present value, so it clearly matters.

questions.q: A council finds that people who chose to attend its job club earn more a year later than people who did not. Why might this overstate the club's effect?
options: Earnings are measured in pounds, which exaggerates differences
Reverse causality: higher earnings caused people to attend the club
Selection bias: the people who chose to attend may have been more motivated or employable anyway
The sample is too small, so the estimate must be biased
questions.why: Attendance was voluntary, so attendees probably differ in motivation or skills that raise earnings anyway, which makes the comparison overstate the club's effect. Reverse causality is unlikely because earnings were measured a year after attendance. A small sample makes an estimate imprecise, but it does not make it biased in one direction. The units of measurement do not create or remove a difference between groups.

questions.q: Explain why the choice of discount rate matters in cost–benefit analysis, using the example of a climate policy whose costs are paid now and whose benefits arrive in 50 years.
markScheme: PV = benefit/(1 + r)^t; discounting reduces the weight on distant benefits
Correct illustration, e.g. £1m in 50 years is worth about £179,000 at 3.5% and £228,000 at 3%
Higher rates make long-term projects look worse; small changes in r have large effects over long horizons
Reasons for discounting: impatience/pure time preference, future generations richer (diminishing marginal utility), risk
Ethical debate over weighting future generations; UK Green Book rate 3.5% and the 2026 review recommending 3%
questions.modelAnswer: Cost–benefit analysis converts future benefits to present values using PV = B/(1 + r)^t. Over long horizons this has a huge effect: £1m of benefits in 50 years is worth about £179,000 today at the Green Book's 3.5% but about £228,000 at 3%, about 27% more. A climate policy that pays costs now and gains benefits in 50 years can therefore pass or fail depending on a small change in r. Economists justify discounting by pure time preference, by the expectation that future generations will be richer so an extra pound is worth less to them, and by risk. But a positive rate of pure time preference means valuing future people less simply because they live later, which many regard as unethical for intergenerational problems. That debate is why the UK commissioned a review of the Green Book rate, which in June 2026 recommended reducing it to 3%.

questions.q: The UK needs 2 hours to make a unit of cloth and 6 hours for a unit of wine; France needs 4 hours for cloth and 8 for wine. Which pattern of specialisation is consistent with comparative advantage?
options: The UK specialises in cloth and France in wine
No trade is beneficial, because the UK has an absolute advantage in both
The UK specialises in both, because it is more productive in both
The UK specialises in wine and France in cloth
questions.why: A unit of wine costs the UK 6/2 = 3 units of cloth but costs France 8/4 = 2, so France has the lower opportunity cost of wine and the UK the lower opportunity cost of cloth. Specialising in both confuses absolute with comparative advantage; the UK cannot use its hours for both at once. Swapping the pattern gets the opportunity cost comparison backwards. Ricardo's point is that trade is beneficial even when one country has an absolute advantage in everything.

questions.q: A small country has demand Qd = 120 − P and supply Qs = P, and imports at a world price of £20. It imposes a £10 tariff. What is the deadweight loss?
questions.why: The price rises to £30, consumption falls from 100 to 90 and production rises from 20 to 30. Consumers lose £950, producers gain £250 and the government collects £600, leaving a net loss of £100. £950 is the consumers' loss alone, ignoring the gains to producers and the government. £600 is the tariff revenue, which is a transfer, not a loss. £50 counts only one of the two triangles, the production or the consumption distortion.

questions.q: If trade creates aggregate gains, why is free trade often politically unpopular? Use economic theory and evidence in your answer.
markScheme: Gains from trade are aggregate but unevenly distributed: consumers/exporters gain, import-competing workers lose
Stolper–Samuelson: scarce factor (e.g. low-skilled labour in rich countries) loses
Evidence: losses concentrated in places, e.g. China shock (Autor, Dorn and Hanson, 2013)
Compensation of losers is possible in principle but often inadequate
Collective action: concentrated losers/producers organise, dispersed gainers do not (Olson); visibility of job losses vs diffuse price gains
questions.modelAnswer: Trade raises total income through specialisation by comparative advantage, but the gains are unevenly shared. Consumers gain from lower prices and exporters from bigger markets, while workers and firms in import-competing industries lose. The Stolper–Samuelson theorem predicts that a country's scarce factor loses: in rich countries, low-skilled labour. The losses are concentrated in particular places: Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2013) found that US areas more exposed to Chinese imports suffered larger falls in manufacturing employment, lower wages and higher benefit take-up, and their later work found these losses persisted. In principle winners could compensate losers, but in practice compensation is limited, so the losers really are worse off. Politically, job losses are visible and concentrated while gains are spread thinly across consumers, so, as Olson's logic of collective action predicts, losers and protected producers organise and lobby more effectively than gainers.

questions.q: Why did automatic enrolment into workplace pensions increase pension saving so much?
options: It removed employers' obligation to contribute
People tend to stick with the default option because of inertia and present bias
It made pension saving compulsory with no opt-out
It greatly increased the tax relief on pension contributions
questions.why: Auto-enrolment changed the default from not saving to saving, and inertia and present bias mean most people do not actively opt out. It was not compulsory: employees can opt out, which is what makes it a nudge. The policy did not work by raising tax relief; the change was in the default. It added an employer contribution obligation rather than removing one.

questions.q: According to the Diamond–Saez approach, which change would lower the revenue-maximising top income tax rate?
options: Closing avoidance routes so that income is harder to shift
A rise in top tax rates in neighbouring countries, which reduces the incentive for top earners to move abroad
A thicker top tail of the income distribution
A larger elasticity of taxable income among top earners
questions.why: The revenue-maximising rate falls as taxable income becomes more responsive, because higher rates then shrink the tax base more. A thicker top tail raises the optimal rate, since there is more income to tax relative to the behavioural cost. Closing avoidance routes lowers the elasticity and so raises the optimal rate. Higher top rates abroad make emigration less attractive, lowering the elasticity of taxable income and so raising, not lowering, the revenue-maximising rate.

questions.q: Using UK workplace pension auto-enrolment as an example, explain what a nudge is and evaluate the use of nudges in public policy.
markScheme: Nudge: change in choice architecture that steers behaviour without removing options or significantly changing incentives (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008)
Auto-enrolment: default switched to saving with opt-out (Pensions Act 2008, from October 2012; 8% minimum total, at least 3% employer)
Mechanism: inertia, present bias, procrastination; participation rose sharply
Strengths: cheap, preserves choice, can be tested with trials
Weaknesses: modest or non-replicating effects in some cases, paternalism concerns, may substitute for structural policy; default contribution levels may be too low
questions.modelAnswer: A nudge alters the way a choice is presented so that people are steered towards a particular option, without banning alternatives or substantially changing financial incentives (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008). UK automatic enrolment, introduced under the Pensions Act 2008 and rolled out from October 2012, switched the default for eligible employees from not saving to saving: they are enrolled unless they opt out, with minimum total contributions of 8% of qualifying earnings, at least 3% from the employer. Because of inertia and present bias, few people opt out, and participation rose sharply. Nudges are attractive because they are cheap, preserve freedom of choice and can be tested in trials. But many have modest effects that fade or fail to replicate at scale; deciding which choice to promote is paternalistic; and a default contribution of 8% may be too low for an adequate retirement, so people who stay at the default may feel falsely reassured. Nudges complement, rather than replace, taxes, regulation and public provision.

questions.q: "Market failure justifies government intervention." Discuss, with reference to at least two types of market failure and to the risk of government failure.
markScheme: Defines market failure as Pareto inefficiency and explains why competitive markets are efficient under ideal conditions
First failure analysed accurately, e.g. negative externality: social cost > private cost, overproduction, Pigouvian tax/permits/regulation, Coase
Second failure analysed accurately, e.g. public goods (free riding) or asymmetric information (adverse selection/moral hazard)
Uses UK examples correctly (e.g. carrier bag charge, UK ETS, compulsory motor insurance, CMA)
Explains government failure: information, capture/lobbying, electoral incentives, public choice, distortionary taxation
Distinguishes necessary from sufficient: compare imperfect markets with imperfect governments; choose the instrument carefully
Recognises equity as a separate justification for intervention and reaches a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Market failure is a strong but not automatic justification for intervention. Under ideal conditions a competitive market is Pareto efficient: every trade worth more to the buyer than it costs to produce takes place. Market failure means those conditions break down so that the outcome is inefficient, and someone could be made better off without anyone being worse off. That creates a potential case for government action, but whether action improves matters depends on what government can achieve.

The first failure is negative externalities. A firm that pollutes ignores the cost to people downwind, so marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost and output is too high. A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal damage, as Pigou proposed in 1920, makes the polluter face the full cost. The UK uses this logic in fuel duty and in the carrier bag charge in England (5p from 2015, 10p from 2021), and it uses tradable permits in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme. Coase (1960) showed that private bargaining could in principle solve the problem without government, but with many affected people and high bargaining costs it rarely does, so intervention is well justified here.

The second failure is public goods. Flood defences are non-rival and non-excludable, so each resident hopes others will pay and voluntary provision falls short. Tax-financed provision is the standard solution. Asymmetric information gives a third example: in insurance, adverse selection can unravel markets, which is why motor insurance is compulsory.

But a failure is necessary rather than sufficient. Governments face their own information problems: the marginal damage of pollution or the value of flood protection is hard to measure. Public choice theory warns that politicians and regulators respond to lobbying, may be captured by the industries they regulate, and favour visible, short-term projects before elections. Intervention is financed by distortionary taxes, each with its own excess burden. Poorly designed policy can therefore leave things worse than the imperfect market.

The right test compares an imperfect market with an imperfect government, case by case. Intervention is most clearly justified where the failure is large, the remedy is well targeted and simple (a tax on a measurable emission), and the risks of capture are low. It is weakest where information is poor and interests are concentrated. Finally, governments also intervene for equity, which is a separate, normative justification: even an efficient market can produce an unacceptable distribution. Market failure is one reason for intervention among several, and it never removes the need to design policy carefully.

questions.q:
A government is considering a flood-defence scheme costing £100m today. It is expected to prevent £12m of damage a year for 10 years, starting next year.
(a) Explain why future benefits are discounted, and calculate the net present value at the Green Book's standard rate of 3.5%. [6]
(b) Recalculate the NPV at 3% and comment on what this means for the decision. [4]
(c) Identify two benefits or costs that a full appraisal should include but the figures above may omit, and explain how they could be valued. [4]
(d) After the scheme is built, how could the government evaluate whether it actually reduced flood damage? Discuss the main difficulty. [6]
markScheme: (a) Reasons for discounting: time preference, future generations richer (diminishing marginal utility), risk/opportunity cost of funds
(b) At 3%: PV ≈ £102.4m, NPV ≈ +£2.4m; decision sensitive to the rate; recent review recommended 3% (June 2026), not necessarily adopted
(c) Two valid omissions, e.g. lives/health, disruption, environmental or amenity effects, maintenance costs, benefits beyond 10 years, distributional weights
(c) Valuation methods: revealed preference (house prices), stated preference (willingness to pay), avoided costs, value of a prevented fatality
(d) Counterfactual problem: damage depends on rainfall; simple before–after misleading
(d) Method: difference-in-differences with similar unprotected areas (parallel trends) or modelling damage conditional on flood events; discuss data and assumptions
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A pound in the future is worth less than a pound today because people prefer consumption sooner (pure time preference), because future generations are expected to be richer, so an extra pound is worth less to them, and because public funds have alternative uses. The present value of £12m a year for 10 years at 3.5% is 12 × [1 − 1.035^−10] ÷ 0.035 = 12 × 8.3166 = £99.8m. NPV = 99.8 − 100 = −£0.2m (more precisely −£0.20m). On these figures the scheme narrowly fails.

(b) At 3%, the annuity factor is [1 − 1.03^−10] ÷ 0.03 = 8.5302, so PV = 12 × 8.5302 = £102.4m and NPV = +£2.4m. The decision flips with a half-point change in the rate, so the result is not robust. The Green Book rate has been 3.5% since 2003, but an independent review published in June 2026 recommended 3%; whether the Treasury adopts it could change decisions on long-lived projects like this. The appraisal should report sensitivity tests and switching values.

(c) The figures probably omit (i) avoided harm to health and life, including stress and injuries during floods, which can be valued with a standard value of a prevented fatality or casualty, and (ii) benefits after year 10, since flood defences typically last much longer; including them would raise the PV substantially. Other candidates are avoided disruption to transport and businesses, valued as avoided costs, and amenity or environmental effects, valued by revealed preference (house prices in protected areas) or stated preference surveys. Maintenance costs should also be added.

(d) The difficulty is the counterfactual: flood damage depends heavily on rainfall, so a simple comparison of damage before and after construction would credit or blame the scheme for the weather. A better design compares the change in damage in the protected area with the change in similar unprotected areas that faced comparable rainfall (difference-in-differences), assuming parallel trends without the scheme. Alternatively, analysts can compare actual damage in specific storms with hydrological model predictions of damage without the defences. Both need good data on damage and weather, and the evaluation may need many years because large floods are rare.
